3.1: Figure 1 shows all randomised participants (23 placebo, 24 400 mg, 23 800 mg) in the final ITT analysis, and 77 of 82 (94%) completed the 4-week treatment, but no report gives how many participants had an observed Cannabis Withdrawal Scale score at week 16 (a follow-up site visit). Table S5 gives raw means without denominators, and the report says missing data were handled by Bayesian multiple imputation, which counts as missing.

3.2: Missing data were handled by Bayesian multiple imputation assuming missing at random within a model with time, baseline score and participant random intercept; no sensitivity analysis to missing-not-at-random assumptions is reported, and such imputation is not assumed to correct bias.

3.3: Loss to follow-up in a cannabis cessation trial could relate to participants' withdrawal symptoms and cannabis use, so missingness could depend on the true score.

3.4: None of the five reasons for a Yes is shown: the few reported dropouts during treatment (1 placebo, 1 in each other arm shown in Figure 1) had reasons such as lost to follow-up, missed visits or psychotropic medication, and no differences in proportions or reasons between arms are reported; "no participants dropped out because of treatment". Week 16 missingness is unreported, so this is a judgement.

5.1: The registry record (first submitted 2014-01-22, before the March 2014 start) lists only a single broad secondary outcome, "Psychological Wellbeing, Cognition and Endocannabinoids", and does not name the Cannabis Withdrawal Scale or week 16. The OSF protocol (https://osf.io/3cbef/) is cited but was not captured, so no dated source shows this scale and time point were fixed before unblinded data. The article describes the scale among planned secondary endpoints, but that is not a dated plan.

5.2: The scale was a single total score, and Table S5 reports the group means at every assessed time point from baseline through week 16 (weeks 20 and 24 not assessed), so no time point appears to have been picked from a larger set. The report states the total score was the one recorded.

5.3: The Result is a descriptive raw-data mean per group and time point, "Summary statistics stratified by treatment group and timepoint were obtained from raw data", so there is essentially one way to compute it, and the model-based contrasts (treatment weeks and all data) were also reported. No evidence suggests alternative analyses were run and withheld.

1.1: The report says a software-generated plan was used in blocks of 12, but then states participants 'were coded consecutively; the first 12 were assigned to P-MPMP, the second 12 to SA-MPMP and the last 12 to SMC'. That is a deterministic assignment by order of entry, not a random order within blocks. Fig 1 further says participants 'chose to be included' in each arm. A random component is therefore doubtful, although the claim of software generation prevents a firm 'No'.

1.2: Assignment followed a fixed order (first 12, then second 12, then last 12), so the enrolling investigators could foresee every forthcoming allocation. No concealment mechanism is described, and the authors state investigators and staff were not blinded to the randomization. Large blocks are acknowledged as a limitation.

1.3: The only reported significant baseline difference is anxiety (P-MPMP higher than SMC, p = 0.047), which fits chance, and no other baseline measure or demographic differed significantly. Baseline RDQ means differ (12.1, 11.2, 8.4) but not significantly. Group sizes at entry are unclear (Fig 1 gives 10, 12, 11 against a planned 12:12:12).

1.1: Page 3 states randomization used a computer-generated randomization list held at the Central Pharmacy, Odense University Hospital. A computer-generated list is a random component.

1.2: Allocation was done by an independent central pharmacy, the list was retained there until after the last 1-year follow-up, and identical placebo/active tablets were packed in sealed boxes labelled only with patient number (1-162). This matches central pharmacy randomization with numbered identical containers. The report does not say explicitly that boxes were dispensed in sequence only after irreversible assignment, so a judgement is needed; Probably yes rather than Yes.

1.3: Table 2 shows balanced age, sex, smoking, pain duration, baseline RMDQ (15 vs 15), back pain (6.7 vs 6.3) and other measures, all NS. The only significant difference is the proportion with minute (grade 1) Modic changes (10.4% vs 28.8%, p=0.007) among about 15 comparisons, which is compatible with chance and not at the P<0.001 level. Group sizes 90 vs 72 reflect the intended four-arm 45/36/45/36 design (2 active : 2 placebo arms, unequal by design).

3.1: 162 randomized; 144 (88.9%) completed the 1-year follow-up. Fig. 1 gives 77/90 (85.6%) antibiotic and 67/72 (93.1%) placebo, so 14.4% and 6.9% of outcome data are missing (13 and 5 dropouts). This is well above the ~5% typically regarded as 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome, and analysis was restricted to 1-year participants with no imputation.

3.2: The analysis was complete-case on 1-year participants. No sensitivity analysis, imputation or weighting for missing outcomes is described in the Methods. The only comparison reported is that lost-to-follow-up participants did not differ by age or gender, but included more smokers; this does not show robustness of the outcome to plausible missing values.

3.3: Reasons for dropout include side effects (4, antibiotic group), new disc herniation (3 antibiotic, 3 placebo), new cancer and no-show. Several are health-related and could relate to back pain/disability status, so missingness could depend on the true outcome value.

3.4: Missing proportions differ between groups (14.4% antibiotic vs 6.9% placebo) and reasons differ: side-effect withdrawals and other health-related exits occurred only in the antibiotic group, while placebo dropouts were new disc herniation and no-shows. New disc herniation and side effects are adverse experiences plausibly tied to pain and disability, and smokers (a prognostic factor) were over-represented among those lost. With about 11% overall missingness, unadjusted complete-case analysis, and a large between-group difference that is sensitive to this, dependence of missingness on outcome is judged likely.
